text: James Orsen Bakker (/ˈbeɪkər/; born January 2, 1940) is an American televangelist and convicted felon. Between 1974 and 1987, he hosted The PTL Club and its cable platform, the PTL Satellite Network, with his then-wife, Tammy Faye. He also developed Heritage USA, a now-defunct Christian theme park in Fort Mill, South Carolina. Born in Muskegon, Michigan, to Raleigh Bakker and Furnia Lynette "Furn" Irwin, Bakker attended North Central University in Minneapolis, a Bible college affiliated with the Assemblies of God, where he met Tammy Faye LaValley in 1960. While working at a restaurant in the Young-Quinlan department store and she at the Three Sisters boutique, he began courting her despite already having a fiancée in Muskegon. The couple married on April 1, 1961, left college, and became itinerant evangelists, having two children: Tammy Sue "Sissy" Bakker Chapman (born March 2, 1970) and Jamie Charles "Jay" Bakker (born December 18, 1975). They divorced on March 13, 1992. Bakker married Lori Beth Graham on September 4, 1998, fifty days after meeting her, and together they adopted five children in 2002, siblings whom Lori had befriended in Phoenix. Early in his career, Bakker worked at Pat Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network (CBN) in Portsmouth, Virginia, helping grow the network and hosting shows including The 700 Club and a children’s program called Come On Over, which used comic routines with puppets. Due to its success, Robertson made Bakker host The 700 Club, which became CBN’s flagship program. The Bakkers left CBN in 1973 and joined Paul and Jan Crouch to co-found the Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) in California, but the partnership lasted only eight months due to disagreements. They then moved to Charlotte, North Carolina, where in May 1973 they launched an east coast version of Praise The Lord under TBN’s umbrella. Less than a year later, they formed their own nonprofit, registered the PTL trademark, left TBN and the Crouches, and continued their show on stations including 36 WRET Charlotte and 16 WGGS Greenville. In 1975, they nationally debuted The PTL Club, and Bakker founded the PTL Satellite Network in 1974 to air the show and other religious programs. Throughout the 1970s, the Bakkers built a headquarters called Heritage Village in the Carolinas and expanded the ministry to include Heritage USA, which became the third most successful theme park in the U.S. at the time. Viewer contributions were estimated to exceed $1 million a week, with proceeds used to expand the park and the ministry’s mission. Bakker stated: "I believe that if Jesus were alive today, he would be on TV." In 1979, PTL came under investigation by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for allegedly misusing funds raised on air. The FCC report, finalized in 1982, found that Bakker raised $350,000 promised for overseas missions but used it for Heritage USA and that the Bakkers used PTL funds for personal expenses. FCC commissioners voted four to three to drop the investigation, allowing Bakker to sell his only TV station and bypass future oversight. The FCC forwarded the report to the U.S. Department of Justice, which declined to press charges due to insufficient evidence. Bakker used the controversy to raise more funds, branding it a "witch-hunt" and asking viewers to "give the Devil a black eye." A confidential 1985 Internal Revenue Service (IRS) report found that $1.3 million in ministry funds was used for the Bakkers’ personal benefit from 1980 to 1983, recommending PTL be stripped of its tax-exempt status, though no action was taken until after the Jessica Hahn scandal broke in 1987. Art Harris and Michael Isikoff wrote in The Washington Post that politics may have played a role, as members of the Reagan administration were reluctant to target evangelical ministers whose followers formed their base. A $279,000 payoff to Jessica Hahn, who alleged that Bakker and former PTL Club co-host John Wesley Fletcher drugged and raped her, was paid with PTL funds through Bakker’s associate Roe Messner. Bakker, who made PTL’s financial decisions, allegedly kept two sets of books to conceal accounting irregularities. Reporters for The Charlotte Observer, led by Charles Shepard, investigated PTL’s finances and published a series of articles. On March 19, 1987, after the disclosure of the Hahn payoff, Bakker resigned from PTL. Although he acknowledged a sexual encounter with Hahn at a hotel in Clearwater, Florida, he denied raping her. He also denied homosexual and bisexual allegations made by Fletcher and PTL director Jay Babcock under oath. Rival televangelist John Ankerberg made allegations of moral impropriety against Bakker on Larry King Live, which both Bakkers denied. Bakker was succeeded as PTL head by Rev. Jerry Falwell of Thomas Road Baptist Church in Lynchburg, Virginia, whom he chose because he feared Jimmy Swaggart was attempting to take over the ministry. Bakker believed Falwell would temporarily lead the ministry until the scandal died down, but on April 28, 1987, Falwell barred Bakker from returning. Later that summer, as donations declined sharply, Falwell raised $20 million to keep Heritage USA solvent and took a promised water slide ride at the park. Falwell and the remaining PTL board members resigned in October 1987, stating that a bankruptcy court ruling made rebuilding the ministry impossible. Falwell called Bakker a liar, an embezzler, a sexual deviant, and "the greatest scab and cancer on the face of Christianity in 2,000 years of church history." On CNN, Swaggart stated that Bakker was a "cancer in the body of Christ." In February 1988, Swaggart became involved in a sex scandal after being caught visiting prostitutes in New Orleans. The Bakker and Swaggart scandals significantly increased media scrutiny of televangelists and their finances. Falwell claimed the scandals had "strengthened broadcast evangelism and made Christianity stronger, more mature and more committed." The PTL Club’s fundraising activities between 1984 and 1987 were reported by The Charlotte Observer, leading to criminal charges. Bakker and his associates sold $1,000 "lifetime memberships" granting buyers an annual three-night stay at a luxury hotel at Heritage USA, with tens of thousands sold but only one 500-room hotel ever completed. The prosecution stated that sales exceeded the funds needed to build the hotel, and much of the money went to Heritage USA’s operating expenses, with Bakker keeping $3.4 million. After a 16-month federal grand jury probe, Bakker was indicted in 1988 on eight counts of mail fraud, 15 counts of wire fraud, and one count of conspiracy. In 1989, after a five-week trial beginning on August 28 in Charlotte, North Carolina, a jury found him guilty on all 24 counts. Judge Robert Daniel Potter sentenced him to 45 years in federal prison and a $500,000 fine. At the Federal Medical Center in Rochester, Minnesota, he shared a cell with activist Lyndon LaRouche and skydiver Roger Nelson. The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld the fraud and conspiracy convictions, voided the 45-year sentence and $500,000 fine, and ordered a new sentencing hearing in February 1991, ruling that Potter’s statement about being "sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers" showed religious bias in sentencing. A sentence-reduction hearing on November 16, 1992, reduced Bakker’s sentence to eight years. In August 1993, he was transferred to a minimum-security federal prison in Jesup, Georgia. He was paroled in July 1994, after serving nearly five years, with his son Jay spearheading a letter-writing campaign for leniency. Celebrity lawyer Alan Dershowitz served as Bakker’s parole attorney, stating he would guarantee Bakker would never again engage in the blend of religion and commerce that led to his conviction. Bakker was released from federal custody on December 1, 1994, owing $6 million to the IRS. In 2003, Bakker began broadcasting The Jim Bakker Show daily at Studio City Café in Branson, Missouri, with his second wife Lori, which is carried on CTN, Daystar, Folk TV, Grace Network (Canada), Daystar Television Canada, GEB America, Hope TV (Canada), Impact Network, WGN, WHT, TCT Network, The Word Network, UpliftTV, and ZLiving networks, with most of his audience receiving it via DirecTV and Dish Network. Bakker condemned prosperity theology and has embraced apocalypticism, with his show focusing on millennial and survivalist themes and selling freeze-dried food such as beans on toast. Elspeth Reeve wrote in The Atlantic that Bakker’s "doomsday survival gear" is overpriced. A man named Jerry Crawford, who credits Bakker with saving his marriage, invested $25 million in a new ministry in Blue Eye, Missouri, named Morningside USA. Production for The Jim Bakker Show moved to Morningside in 2008. In 2013, Bakker wrote Time Has Come: How to Prepare Now for Epic Events Ahead about end-time events. He has changed his views on prosperity theology; in his 1980 book Eight Keys to Success, he stated, "God wants you to be happy, God wants you to be rich, God wants you to prosper," and in his 1996 book I Was Wrong, he admitted that the first time he read the Bible all the way through was in prison and that he had taken passages out of context to support his prosperity theology. Bakker now says that "PTL" stands for "Prophets Talking Loud." In an October 2017 video, he said that "God will punish those" who ridicule him; he claimed Hurricane Harvey was a judgment of God and blamed Hurricane Matthew on then-President Barack Obama. He predicted that if then-President Donald Trump was impeached, Christians would begin a Second American Civil War. He compared the 2017 Washington train derailment to the sinking of the RMS Titanic and stated the Amtrak derailment was a warning from God. He also claimed to have predicted the September 11 attacks of 2001, stating he "saw 9/11 in 1999 before New Year's Eve" and that there would be terrorism in New York City and Washington, D.C. A few days after the Stoneman Douglas High School shooting, he stated that "God came to [him] in a dream... and he was wearing camouflage, a hunting vest and had an AR-15 strapped to his back" and that God supported Trump’s plan to arm teachers. Following the death of Billy Graham on February 21, 2018, Bakker attended his funeral and paid his respects, stating Graham was the greatest preacher since Jesus and that Graham had visited him in prison. On the Stand in the Gap Today radio program, Pennsylvania Pastors Network president Sam Rohrer criticized Bakker’s civil-war prediction. Christian Today criticized Bakker’s show for preying on "the most vulnerable kinds of people" and claimed it had "no place on our TV screens." Bakker sold colloidal silver supplements he advertised as a panacea. In March 2020, the office of the Attorney General of New York ordered Bakker to cease making false medicinal claims about his supplements’ alleged ability to cure the 2019–2020 strains of coronavirus, and the Federal Trade Commission and the Food and Drug Administration sent a warning letter to Bakker about his claims regarding the supplements and coronavirus. Missouri attorney general Eric Schmitt and Arkansas attorney general Leslie Rutledge filed lawsuits against Bakker for allegedly promoting the supplements as a treatment for the virus. In the state lawsuit, Bakker is represented by former Missouri governor Jay Nixon, who argued for dismissal, stating the allegations are false and that Bakker is being unfairly targeted by those seeking to crush his ministry and force his program off the air. In April 2020, prohibited from receiving credit card transactions, Bakker disclosed to his viewers.

Jim Bakker promoted colloidal silver supplements that he claimed could cure various illnesses, including the 2019–2020 strains of coronavirus. In March 2020, the New York Attorney General ordered Bakker to stop making false medical claims about the supplements' ability to treat the coronavirus, and both the Federal Trade Commission and the Food and Drug Administration issued a warning letter to him regarding those claims. Missouri Attorney General Eric Schmitt and Arkansas Attorney General Leslie Rutledge filed lawsuits against Bakker for allegedly promoting the supplements as a coronavirus treatment. In the state lawsuit, Bakker was represented by former Missouri governor Jay Nixon, who argued the allegations were false and claimed Bakker was being unfairly targeted by those seeking to shut down his Christian television program. In April 2020, Bakker was prohibited from accepting credit card transactions and disclosed to his viewers that his ministry was facing bankruptcy, urgently asking for donations. The following month, GEB America and World Harvest Television removed Bakker's program from their networks after DirecTV owner AT&T requested channels to reconsider airing the show, in response to a deplatforming campaign by the liberal Christian group Faithful America. On May 8, 2020, Lori Bakker announced that Jim Bakker had suffered a minor stroke, which she attributed to his intense work schedule and described as the most vicious criticism he had ever faced; she stated he would take a sabbatical until recovery. Bakker returned to his program for the first time after the stroke on July 8, 2020. On June 23, 2021, Missouri Attorney General Eric Schmitt announced a settlement of the state lawsuit, which prohibited Bakker and Morningside Church from claiming that silver solution could diagnose, prevent, mitigate, treat, or cure any disease or illness. As part of the settlement, approximately $157,000 in restitution was paid to individuals who purchased the silver solution between February 12, 2020, and March 10, 2020.
